why-workbooks.q: According to the lesson, what is the new skill that lets a non-coder build software?
options: Saying what you want and judging what comes back
Learning enough syntax to read the agent's code
Memorizing the names of common frameworks and tools
Configuring servers and budgets before you begin
why-workbooks.explain: The lesson says you cross the gap by getting good at saying what you want and judging the result, not by becoming an engineer.

why-workbooks.q: The lesson describes Workbooks not as one product but as what?
options: A subscription service that hosts your finished apps
An ecosystem: a way to hold software, an engine, and agents
A programming language designed for plain-English input
A single app you log into to manage your projects
why-workbooks.explain: It states Workbooks isn't one product you adopt but an ecosystem: a way to hold software, an engine to run it, and agents that build.

why-workbooks.q: What is the lesson's answer to an organization's fear of letting AI touch real systems?
options: Trust the agent because modern models rarely make errors
Keep a human watching every single command the agent runs
The agent runs in a sandbox you own, with revocable powers
Limit the agent to reading data and never writing anything
why-workbooks.explain: The bet is the opposite of trusting the agent: it runs inside a sandbox you own with deliberate, revocable powers and secrets kept off the computer.

why-workbooks.q: Why does the lesson call this 'the durable shape' rather than just an AI tool?
options: Because the agents improve faster than any rival product
Because a company guarantees it will support the format forever
Because it hides its complexity behind a polished interface
Because it's built on standards that outlived a dozen trends
why-workbooks.explain: It's steadier than an AI tool because every part rests on lasting standards: an ordinary file, a plain format, an engine you can run yourself.

why-workbooks.q: For a team, what is the 'quiet idea' underneath Workbooks?
options: Work can travel as one thing that explains itself on arrival
Every tool a team uses should be replaced by a single vendor
Slack threads should be the permanent record of every decision
Teams should grant the agent access to all six of their services
why-workbooks.explain: The idea is that a piece of work, its screen, data, and history can travel as one thing you hand off, explaining itself on arrival.

why-you-can-build-now.q: The lesson says the wall to building software is gone primarily because of what change?
options: Coding languages became dramatically simpler to learn
The job changed: you describe and an agent does the building
Hiring an engineer is now far cheaper than it used to be
Computers got fast enough to write their own programs alone
why-you-can-build-now.explain: It states the wall is gone because the job changed: you describe what you want and an agent builds it, not because coding got easier.

why-you-can-build-now.q: In the tip-calculator example, what did the user notably leave out of the prompt?
options: Who the tool was for and what feeling it should have
The exact tip percentages the calculator should offer
How it should be built and which technology to use
Any request that the numbers be easy to read on a phone
why-you-can-build-now.explain: The lesson highlights that the prompt described the outcome and audience but never said how, or named a single piece of technology.

why-you-can-build-now.q: How does the lesson say a non-coder can direct something they can't read?
options: By learning to skim the code for obvious errors first
By trusting the agent's own description of what it built
By giving the agent extremely detailed technical instructions
By judging the result, the way an editor judges a writer
why-you-can-build-now.explain: You direct by judging the result, not the method, the way an editor directs a writer or a client directs a designer.

why-you-can-build-now.q: According to the lesson, what makes the sandbox the part 'that makes this sane'?
options: The agent can't reach the rest of your machine from it
The agent promises not to touch your files or passwords
It backs up your real computer before the agent runs
It scans the agent's work for dangerous commands first
why-you-can-build-now.explain: Safety comes from the shape of the room: a sealed workspace the agent can't reach out of, so there's nothing of yours to break.

why-you-can-build-now.q: What is the lesson's honest framing of what Workbooks is?
options: A tool that runs itself once you set it up correctly
Software built in workbooks, by people and agents together
An app you log into where agents work without supervision
A way to finally make the human director optional
why-you-can-build-now.explain: The lesson insists it is software built in workbooks by people and agents together, not software that runs itself while you walk away.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: The lesson says the most important skill for a first request is what?
options: Knowing a programming language well enough to check work
Writing a complete, flawless spec before you ever send it
Asking well: saying clearly what you want a capable builder to do
Spelling out the exact steps the agent should follow
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: It frames the key skill as the old human skill of asking well, saying what you want clearly enough that someone capable can do it.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: Why is the to-do-list request better than the flexbox-and-divs request?
options: It is far longer and lists more technical requirements
It tells the agent exactly which sorting function to write
It names a popular layout the agent should always prefer
It describes the outcome, so the agent can pick a better road
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The second is shorter and better because it gives purpose, audience, and feel, letting the agent choose a better construction than you'd spell out.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: Which of these does the lesson present as a key thing a first request should include?
options: How you'll know it worked, a finish line you can check
A list of the specific files the agent should create
The framework and database the agent ought to choose
A guess at the layout so the agent doesn't have to decide
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The four things a new colleague would need include 'how will you know it worked' — a finish line the agent can aim at and you can check.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: What rule does the lesson tell you to carry away about quality?
options: Magic phrasing matters more than the detail you provide
Vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out
Always keep requests as short as possibly can be
Technical wording produces a more specific result
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The rule is 'vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out' — detail about the outcome is the biggest lever on result quality.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: What does the lesson mean when it says 'specific does not mean technical'?
options: You should add code only after the first draft comes back
Technical detail is fine as long as it's also very specific
Rich, specific description of the outcome can use no code at all
Specific requests must name at least one piece of technology
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The better dog-walking request had not one word of code; being richly specific about the outcome while staying out of construction is the move.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: What does the lesson say experienced people actually have that beginners lack?
options: A secret set of magic words that produce perfect output
The ability to read and fix the agent's code themselves
A better, more detailed first prompt than everyone else
A loop they trust: say it, look hard, say the next thing
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: There are no magic words; experienced people have a loop they trust — say what they want, look hard, redirect — run over and over.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: What are the three beats of the loop, in order?
options: Prompt, Look, Redirect
Plan, Build, Deploy
Describe, Wait, Accept
Ask, Approve, Repeat
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: The loop has three beats run in order: Prompt (say what you want), Look (examine what came back), Redirect (name what's off).

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: Which beat does the lesson warn people most often skip, causing projects to go wrong?
options: The prompt, because people overthink the wording
The look, actually examining whether it's really right
The redirect, because corrections feel confrontational
The restart, because people refuse to begin again
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: Look is the beat people skip — actually examining whether it is right, not whether it sounds right — and skipping it is where projects go wrong.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: In the pottery-workshop example, what made the redirect effective?
options: It re-explained the entire project from the beginning
It told the agent to make the whole thing better overall
It named exactly what was seen: a notes box and remaining spots
It started over rather than building on the prior version
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: The redirect worked because it named the specific results seen — add a notes box, show remaining spots — giving the agent concrete targets.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: Why does the lesson say it's safe to run a tight loop fast?
options: Because the agent rarely makes a wrong turn in practice
Because a human approves each change before it is saved
Because bold redirects are tested in a separate copy first
Because the workbook records its history, so you can undo
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: It's safe because a workbook keeps its own history with a way back, so the cost of a bad lap is just one more lap.

reading-what-it-did.q: What mindset does the lesson recommend taking toward the agent?
options: A talented, fast, slightly overconfident colleague to verify
An infallible oracle whose output you can safely accept
An enemy that is probably trying to deceive you each time
A junior who needs every step spelled out in advance
reading-what-it-did.explain: Treat the agent as a talented, fast, slightly overconfident colleague on their first week — verify the work rather than assume it.

reading-what-it-did.q: Why does the lesson call 'it looks fine' a coin flip?
options: Because skimming takes longer than a proper review does
Because confident fiction and wrong-thing-done-well look correct
Because the agent always hides its mistakes deliberately
Because reading the agent's description is enough to be sure
reading-what-it-did.explain: Two mistakes sail through a skim — confident fiction and doing the wrong thing well — because both produce output that looks like correct work.

reading-what-it-did.q: What is 'drift' as the lesson defines it?
options: The agent slowing down as a project grows larger
A dramatic failure where the agent crashes mid-task
Slowly solving a slightly different problem than yours
The agent forgetting earlier parts of the conversation
reading-what-it-did.explain: Drift is the agent slowly solving a slightly different problem than the one you have, accumulating small wrong turns that each looked reasonable.

reading-what-it-did.q: What makes the ledger a record the agent 'can't fake'?
options: The agent reviews and signs the log before it is sealed
A second agent rewrites the log to confirm it is honest
The agent chooses which steps are important enough to record
The system writes each action at a chokepoint, then seals it
reading-what-it-did.explain: The agent doesn't hold the pen; the system records every action at a chokepoint and seals the log, so any later edit breaks the stamp.

reading-what-it-did.q: What does the lesson say the best evals are?
options: Traps that plant the exact mistake this task tends to make
Checklists that confirm every feature is present and working
Final-answer graders that read only the agent's conclusion
One-time reviews you run by hand on each individual change
reading-what-it-did.explain: The best evals aren't checklists, they're traps: you plant the exact mistake the task tends to make, and a pass means the agent didn't bite.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What is the whole skill Dana brings, according to the lesson?
options: A little hidden coding ability she rarely admits to
Describing clearly what she wants, like briefing a new hire
Knowing which framework and database to choose up front
Reading the agent's code closely to catch its errors
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Dana can't code; her whole skill is describing what she wants clearly, the way she'd brief a sharp new hire.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What did the agent do after reading Dana's first brief?
options: Silently guessed at the unclear parts and built immediately
Returned a wall of code for Dana to review line by line
Asked two decisions that change the result: live-update and dropdowns
Refused to start until Dana provided a complete spec
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: The agent showed up as a collaborator, finding the two decisions that change the result — live updates and dropdown vs. free text — and asking.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: When Dana reviews the tool, what is she actually judging?
options: The quality and structure of the underlying code
Whether the agent's description sounds accurate
How fast the agent finished the build
The result against what she asked for, like any draft
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Dana doesn't read code; she reviews the result against what she asked for, and is more qualified than the agent because she knows her team.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What are the 'three levels' the lesson names for the agent?
options: It answers, it checks itself, it works with you over time
It plans, it codes, it deploys without your involvement
It listens, it remembers, it eventually runs on its own
It drafts, it tests, it replaces the human director
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: The three levels are: Level 1 it answers, Level 2 it checks itself, Level 3 it works with you over time as a collaborator.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What does the lesson say about putting Dana's workbook on the web?
options: It requires rebuilding the tool for a different environment
It's closer to flipping one setting than the dreaded deploy
It demands a separate hosting account and a build step
It only works after engineers review the whole project
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Going live is closer to flipping one setting than the white-knuckle deploy engineers dread; the same thing runs, just somewhere else.

the-one-file.q: What is the core unit of everything in Workbooks, per the lesson?
options: The runtime server that hosts and scales the projects
The org layer that records the intent and the tasks
A workbook, which at first glance looks like an HTML page
The SQLite database that holds the saved data
the-one-file.explain: The thing you walk away with is a workbook, the core unit; it looks like a web page, an .html file, the format the internet is built on.

the-one-file.q: What does the lesson correct about 'a workbook is just one HTML file'?
options: A workbook is actually a proprietary archive, not HTML
A workbook can't run without being connected to a server
A workbook is only the visible screen, never the data
When it travels it's a small bundle, and the bundle is the unit
the-one-file.explain: The first correction: a workbook is not only a single HTML file; when it travels it's a small bundle, and the bundle is what you own and send.

the-one-file.q: Which four standards are bound into the workbook bundle?
options: HTML, SQLite, org, and a one-line manifest
HTML, JSON, Python, and a config file
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a database driver
HTML, zip, Elixir, and a manifest
the-one-file.explain: The bundle binds four standards: workbook.html for the face, vfs.sqlite for the disk, workbook.org for the why, and manifest.json to bind them.

the-one-file.q: What does the lesson identify as the over-claim it wants to retire?
options: That a workbook is a plain zip you can open with unzip
That single workbooks can open and run on their own
That a workbook is self-contained, so there's no server
That the bundle's formats are boring and openable
the-one-file.explain: The claim to retire is 'no server': a single workbook runs alone, but for agents, other languages, or scale it stands on a runtime.

the-one-file.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between the file and the runtime?
options: The runtime replaces the file once a project gets large
The file and runtime are two competing ways to ship software
The file is the unit you hold; the runtime is the ground it stands on
The runtime is bundled inside every single workbook file
the-one-file.explain: The workbook is the core unit you hold and hand off; the runtime is the ground it stands on when you want more than a single page.
